title: Krylov complexity of a tilted extended Bose-Hubbard chain with Rydberg-dressed interactions
authors: Yifan Chen, Tianyi Yan, Lu Qin, Weibin Li
abstract: We investigate Krylov state complexity in a tilted extended Bose-Hubbard chain in which both the on-site interaction $U$ and nearest-neighbor interaction $V$ are present. The tilted extended Bose-Hubbard model can be realized with Rydberg-dressed interactions in optical lattices. Using exact diagonalization and Lanczos recursion from three physically motivated Fock states, we compute the time-dependent complexity, its long-time saturation value, and the fluctuations of the Lanczos coefficients for an open chain at unit filling. Crucially, we identify a pronounced quasi-chaotic diagonal regime near $U\simeq V$ in which the Krylov complexity saturation exhibits a sharp ridge while the spectral level-spacing statistics remain partially chaotic. This dissociation arises from the competition between the on-site and nearest-neighbor interaction, which generates a dense manifold of near-resonant many-body configurations that is efficiently coupled by the state-dependent dynamics but retains residual spectral structure. Our results show that Krylov state complexity provides complementary, state-sensitive information about many-body chaos that is not captured by the spectral diagnostics alone, establishing Krylov complexity as a useful diagnostic for studying thermalization and information scrambling in experimentally accessible quantum simulators.
summary: This paper investigates quantum chaos in a tilted extended Bose-Hubbard chain simulated with Rydberg-dressed interactions. By calculating Krylov state complexity, the authors demonstrate that this diagnostic provides unique, state-sensitive information about information scrambling. They identify a distinct quasi-chaotic regime where complexity signals differ significantly from traditional spectral measures.
main_problem: The study investigates Krylov state complexity as a state-sensitive diagnostic tool to characterize many-body chaos, thermalization, and information scrambling in quantum many-body systems.
main_result: The authors found a pronounced quasi-chaotic diagonal regime near $U \simeq V$ where Krylov complexity shows a sharp ridge, demonstrating that this diagnostic provides information beyond what is captured by standard spectral diagnostics alone.
method: The analysis employs exact diagonalization and Lanczos recursion to compute time-dependent Krylov state complexity and compare it against spectral level-spacing statistics.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a one-dimensional, tilted extended Bose-Hubbard chain, which is physically realizable using Rydberg-dressed interactions in optical lattices.
key_observables: Krylov state complexity ($C_K(t)$), long-time saturation value ($\langle C_{sat} angle$), spectral level-spacing statistics, and Kullback–Leibler (KL) Divergence.
important_parameters: The competition between on-site interaction ($U$) and nearest-neighbor interaction ($V$), and the ratio $U/V$ near the quasi-chaotic regime.
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed in the fixed-N sector, and a weak linear tilt ($F=0.1J$) is applied to avoid Wannier–Stark localization.
figures_summary: Figures compare Krylov complexity saturation ($C_{sat}^K$) against spectral diagnostics ($	ext{KL}_{	ext{POI}}$ and $\langle e_D^{(1)} angle$) across the $(U/J, V/J)$ plane, highlighting the distinct signature of the diagonal ridge in $C_{sat}^K$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the model and the diagnostic tools, calculates the time evolution using Lanczos recursion, and then presents comparative results showing the unique information provided by Krylov complexity versus spectral measures across different interaction regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced quantum chaos diagnostics (Krylov complexity) to a highly relevant and experimentally accessible platform (Rydberg-dressed Bose-Hubbard model), providing a powerful new tool for understanding thermalization in quantum simulators.
